pages.md: # Macro Graph of Experts for Billion-Scale Multi-Task Recommendation Hongyu Yao * Jinan University Guangzhou, China hongyuya0666@gmail.com Zijin Hong * The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Hong Kong SAR, China zijin.hong@connect.polyu.hk Hao Chen† City University of Macau Macau SAR, China sundaychenhao@gmail.com Yuanchen Bei Zhejiang University Zhejiang, China yuanchenbei@zju.edu.cn Zhiqing Li South China Agricultural University Guangzhou, China zhiqinglizzy@gmail.com Qijie Shen Alibaba Group Hangzhou, China qjshenxdu@gmail.com Zuobin Ying City University of Macau Macau SAR, China zbying@cityu.edu.mo Huan Gong National University of Defense Technology Changsha, China gongh15@outlook.com Feiran Huang Jinan University Guangzhou, China huangfr@jnu.edu.cn ## ABSTRACT Graph-based multi-task learning at billion-scale presents a significant challenge, as different tasks correspond to distinct billion-scale graphs. Traditional multi-task learning methods often neglect these graph structures, relying solely on individual user and item embed-dings. However, disregarding graph structures overlooks substantial potential for improving performance. In this paper, we introduce the Macro Graph of Expert (MGOE) framework, the first approach capable of leveraging macro graph embeddings to capture task-specific macro features while modeling the correlations between task-specific experts. Specifically, we propose the concept of a Macro Graph Bottom, which, for the first time, enables multi-task learning models to incorporate graph information effectively. We design the Macro Prediction Tower to dynamically integrate macro knowledge across tasks. MGOE has been deployed at scale, powering multi-task learning for the homepage of a leading billion-scale recommender system. Extensive offline experiments conducted on three public benchmark datasets demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art multi-task learning methods, establishing MGOE as a breakthrough in multi-task graph-based recommendation. Furthermore, online A/B tests confirm the superiority of MGOE in billion-scale recommender systems. ## KEYWORDS multi-task learning, graph neural networks, billion-scale recommender system, click-through rate prediction ## 1 INTRODUCTION Multi-task learning (MTL) lies at the core of nearly all billion-scale recommendation systems \( \left\lbrack {2,{24},{43}}\right\rbrack \) ,responsible for predicting multiple key tasks such as clicks,likes,and adding to cart \( \left\lbrack {{22},{59}}\right\rbrack \) . Its goal is to address multiple tasks in real-time to meet diverse user needs. Previous multi-task recommendation models overlook the valuable information embedded within graphs. As shown in Figure 1, their embedding-based multi-task bottoms rely solely on individual user and item embeddings and disregard the rich relational semantics encoded in graph structures, which ultimately results in suboptimal performance. However, incorporating graph structures in MTL presents greater challenges compared to single-task situations due to two primary reasons: 1) online systems have billions of users and items, necessitating efficient and effective handling of this scale, and 2) multiple graph relations are formed by different tasks, requiring appropriate graph management techniques. The mainstream approach in industrial recommendation typically employs single embeddings for multi-task problems without considering graph structures [31, 32]. ESMM [27] enhances the robustness and improves the overall performance by utilizing the entire exposed sample space for training. MMoE [26] pioneers the use of a basic mixture-of-experts structure, enabling task-specific predictions to learn from other tasks. PLE [36] separates task-sharing and task-specific experts to avoid the negative transfer and seesaw phenomenon. STEM [34] introduces a novel shared and task-specific embeddings paradigm to effectively capture user preferences. Subsequent works focused on designing more sophisticated expert structures, such as multi-layer or task-specialized experts. Other studies explore graph-based multi-task learning; for example, MoGENet [18] proposes a multi-channel graph neural networks (GNNs) to model high-order information using user-item bipartite graphs. MMoCEG [48] introduces graph-based MoE to recognize the commonalities and differences among multiple regions. However, graph-based MTL models often struggle with the high computational burden of GNNs when facing billion-scale graphs. In general, current multi-task learning models face trade-offs in billion-scale recommender systems: 1. Lack of High-Order Information: Graph neural networks have demonstrated significant performance improvements, but single-embedding MTL approaches cannot benefit from extracting and aggregating high-order information. --- "Both authors contributed equally to this research. † Corresponding author. ---

(c) Macro Graph MTL introduces macro graph bottom to incorporate macro graph information. 2. Computational Complexity: Since each task forms a different graph, managing multiple billion-scale graphs introduces considerable computational overhead for online recommendation systems. Considering these trade-offs, designing a billion-scale graph neural network structure that addresses multi-task learning scenarios is a promising direction. Recently, MacGNN [4] introduced a macro graph structure for single click-through rate (CTR) prediction tasks. However, applying macro structures to multi-task learning presents the following challenges: 1. Multi-task Graph Design: Designing appropriate graph structures to capture and integrate information from multiple tasks is a complex challenge. 2. Macro Expert Design: Developing experts capable of learning graph information to predict different tasks requires careful consideration and architectural innovation. 3. Inter-Macro Merging: Efficiently merging information across macro structures is crucial for effective multi-task learning. To address these challenges, we introduce Macro Graph of Experts (MGOE), the first graph neural network architecture for billion-scale multi-task recommendation that avoids introducing unbearable computational complexity. We present the Macro Task Merging Graph (MTMG), which extracts multi-task information using a single macro graph. We then describe the design of macro graph experts that learn graph information to predict different tasks. Finally, we introduce the Macro Prediction Tower, which aggregates multi-level information to simultaneously predict multiple tasks. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: - We pioneer the use of graph neural networks for billion-scale multi-task recommendation, solving the computational complexity challenges of GNNs in real-world applications. - We present the design of MTMG that incorporate multiple different graphs, fundamentally addressing the inability of existing multi-task models to utilize graph information. - We provide implementation details for deploying MGOE in a real-world billion-scale recommender system. - Extensive offline experiments conducted on three public benchmark datasets verify that MGOE outperforms both embedding-based multi-task learning models and graph-based recommendation models. Besides, online A/B test have confirmed the superiority of MGOE in the billion-scale recommender systems. ## 2 PRELIMINARIES ### 2.1 Notations In this paper,we use \( \mathcal{U},\mathcal{I} \) ,and \( \mathcal{T} \) to denote the user set,item set, and task set,respectively. Each task \( t \in \mathcal{T} \) is associated with a task-specific interaction matrix \( {\mathbf{R}}^{\left( t\right) } \) . For any user \( u \in \mathcal{U} \) and item \( i \in \mathcal{I} \) ,the entry \( {r}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } \in {\mathrm{R}}^{\left( t\right) } \) represents the interaction between \( u \) , \( i \) ,and \( t \) . Specifically, \( {r}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } = 1 \) indicates that user \( u \) and item \( i \) have interacted in task \( t \) ,while \( {r}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } = 0 \) implies no interaction. For each task \( t \) ,we have a dataset \( {\mathcal{D}}_{t} \) ,where each element is represented as \( \left( {u,i,{y}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) }}\right) \in {\mathcal{D}}_{t} \) . Here,the label \( {y}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } \in \{ 0,1\} \) indicates whether user \( u \) interacted (1) or did not interact (0) with item \( i \) in task \( t \) . ### 2.2 Multi-task Learning Multi-task learning (MTL) aims to develop the ability to handle multiple related but distinct tasks simultaneously. In e-commerce scenarios, these tasks may involve predicting whether a user will interact with an item by performing a specific behavior, such as clicking on a product, adding it to a cart, or making a purchase. The objective of MTL is to learn a set of functions \( \mathcal{F} \) ,where each function \( {f}_{t} \in \mathcal{F} \) takes user and item features as input to predict the probability of the corresponding task,which is defined as \( {f}_{t}\left( \cdot \right) : \left( {u,i}\right) \rightarrow {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } \) , with \( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } \in \left\lbrack {0,1}\right\rbrack \) representing the predicted probability. Typically, MTL employs the binary cross-entropy loss as the loss function for each task \( t \) ,which is expressed as: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{t} = - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {u,i,{y}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) }}\right) \in {\mathcal{D}}_{t}}}\left\lbrack {{y}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) }\log \left( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) }\right) + \left( {1 - {y}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) }}\right) \log \left( {1 - {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) }}\right) }\right\rbrack .\] The overall loss function \( {\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{{MTL}}} \) is then defined as: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{{MTL}}} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t \in \mathcal{T}}}{\alpha }_{t}{\mathcal{L}}_{t} \tag{1}\] where \( {\alpha }_{t} \) is the parameter to reflect task \( t \) ’s relative importance. ### 2.3 MTL Bottom Embedding-based bottom. The embedding-based MTL bottom serves as the process that transforms feature inputs into fused representations. Typically, for each task, the multi-task bottom takes relevant user micro features \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u} \) and item micro features \( {\mathbf{e}}_{i} \) as input,concatenating them into a vector \( \mathbf{z} = \left\lbrack {{\mathbf{e}}_{u};{\mathbf{e}}_{i}}\right\rbrack \) . This newly formed vector is the input for subsequent expert layers, enabling further feature fusion. Suppose the number of shared experts and task-specific experts is \( {N}_{1} \) and \( {N}_{2} \) ,respectively. The prediction \( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } \) for task \( t \) is then expressed as: \[{h}_{t}\left( z\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 1}}^{{N}_{1}}{\mathrm{G}}_{t,l}^{\left( 1\right) }\left( z\right) {\mathrm{E}}_{s,l}\left( z\right) + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{l = 1}}^{{N}_{2}}{\mathrm{G}}_{t,l}^{\left( 2\right) }\left( \mathrm{z}\right) {\mathrm{E}}_{t,l}\left( z\right) ; \tag{2}\] \[{\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } = \sigma \left( {{\operatorname{MLP}}_{t}\left( {{h}_{t}\left( z\right) }\right) }\right) , \tag{3}\]

where \( \sigma \) denotes the sigmoid function, \( {\mathrm{E}}_{s,l} \) represent the \( l \) -th shared experts, \( {\mathrm{E}}_{t,l} \) is the \( l \) -th task-specific experts for task \( t,{\mathrm{G}}_{t,l}^{\left( 1\right) }\left( \cdot \right) \) and \( {\mathrm{G}}_{t,l}^{\left( 2\right) }\left( \cdot \right) \) represent the gating network operations that fuse the outputs from shared experts and task-specific experts, respectively. It is worth noting that embedding-based MTL models separately focus on user and item micro features, neglecting the graph information formed by user-item interactions. Figure 2: An illustration of the construction of Macro Task Merging Graph and the overview of Macro Graph of Experts. Graph-based bottom. The graph-based bottom typically captures the user-item collaborative connections through graph neural networks (GNNs). Given the input of the \( l \) -th layer \( {\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{l} \) for a certain user/item node \( v \) ,the output of \( \left( {l + 1}\right) \) -th layer \( {\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{l + 1} \) and the prediction \( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } \) for task \( t \) are represented as: \[{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{l + 1} = \operatorname{GNN}\left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{l},\sigma \left( {{\mathbf{W}}_{{\mathcal{G}}_{t}} \cdot \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{c \in \mathcal{N}\left( v\right) }}{\eta }_{v \leftarrow c} \cdot {\mathbf{e}}_{c}^{l}}\right) }\right) ; \tag{4}\] \[{\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( t\right) } = \sigma \left( {{\operatorname{MLP}}_{t}\left( \left\lbrack {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{l + 1};{\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{l + 1}}\right\rbrack \right) }\right) , \tag{5}\] where \( {\mathbf{W}}_{{\mathcal{G}}_{t}} \) is the weight matrix for the task graph \( {\mathcal{G}}_{t} \) ,and \( {\eta }_{v \leftarrow c} \) is implemented using an attention mechanism. Here, \( \mathcal{N}\left( v\right) \) denotes the set of neighbors of node \( v \) . However,when dealing with billion-scale task graphs, the graph-based bottom faces significant challenges in computational resources. ## 3 METHODOLOGY The overall framework of our proposed MGOE is shown in Figure 2. We begin by introducing the macro task merging graph (MTMG) utilized in this paper. Subsequently, we present our proposed MGOE, which is designed to effectively leverage the macro graph information to enhance recommendation performance. ### 3.1 Macro Task Merging Graph In this section, we focus on constructing MTMG, which provides crucial macro graph information for the subsequent MGOE. The construction of MTMG primarily involves two core steps: first, obtaining a merging interaction matrix, and second, computing the macro nodes and constructing the macro edges, respectively. Merging Interaction Matrix. In real-world recommendation scenarios, multiple tasks often coexist (e.g., users may click and purchase an item simultaneously). These task combinations represent the co-existence of various interaction patterns between users and items, reflecting different degrees of user preference. To accurately capture these preferences, we introduce a scoring function to quantify the importance of such task combinations. For any user \( u \in \mathcal{U} \) and item \( i \in \mathcal{I} \) ,the possible task combinations set between them are denoted as: \[{\mathbf{C}}_{ui} = \left\{ {\left( {u,i,{t}_{{j}_{1}}}\right) ,\left( {u,i,{t}_{{j}_{2}}}\right) ,\ldots ,\left( {u,i,{t}_{{j}_{k}}}\right) \mid {t}_{{j}_{1}},{t}_{{j}_{2}},\ldots ,{t}_{{j}_{k}} \in \mathcal{T}}\right\} .\] Let \( C = \left\{ {{\mathrm{C}}_{ui} \mid u \in \mathcal{U},i \in \mathcal{I}}\right\} \) . Once we have defined the importance order of each task, we can obtain a rank function for task combination sets [53],denoted as \( \rho \left( \cdot \right) : C \rightarrow {\mathbb{N}}^{ + } \) . We further define a scoring function \( g\left( \cdot \right) : C \rightarrow \mathbb{R} \) ,which assigns a merging preference score to each task combination, representing its relative importance. Specifically,the merging preference score \( {s}_{ui} \) between user \( u \) and item \( i \) is defined as: \[{s}_{ui} = g\left( {\mathrm{C}}_{ui}\right) = \left\{ {\begin{array}{ll} \frac{{\left\lbrack \rho \left( {\mathrm{C}}_{ui}\right) + 1\right\rbrack }^{\beta } - 1}{\beta } & ,\text{ if }\beta \neq 0 \\ \ln \left\lbrack {\rho \left( {\mathrm{C}}_{ui}\right) + 1}\right\rbrack & ,\text{ if }\beta = 0 \end{array},}\right. \tag{6}\] where \( \beta \) is a transformation parameter used to adjust the importance of task combination sets. Then, we arrange these values corresponding to user-item pairs to construct the merging interaction matrix S: \[\mathrm{S} = {\left\lbrack {s}_{ui}\right\rbrack }_{m \times n} \tag{7}\]

where \( {s}_{ui} \) serves as each entry of the matrix, \( m = \left| \mathcal{U}\right| \) and \( n = \left| \mathcal{I}\right| \) denotes the number of users and items respectively. The well-designed scoring function enables systematic quantitative evaluations of different task combinations, ensuring that the constructed MTMG effectively captures the complex interactions between users and items. This, in turn, supports the efficient operation of the MGOE. Following the definition of the scoring function, we proceed to construct the nodes and edges within MTMG. Macro Node Computation. Computing a macro node involves leveraging the merging preference score computed by Equation 6. Existing approaches treat all nodes in the macro graph uniformly, ignoring the rich semantic relationships in different task combinations. To overcome this limitation, we propose Preference-Based Grouping, a novel method that assigns distinct weights to each micro-node based on its merging preference score. Specifically, we construct macro nodes from two complementary perspectives. Let \( {\mathrm{S}}^{\mathcal{U}} = {\mathrm{{SS}}}^{\top } \) and \( {\mathrm{S}}^{\mathcal{I}} = {\mathrm{S}}^{\top }\mathrm{S} \) . Then we can obtain macro nodes of by performing clustering on users and items based on \( {\mathrm{S}}^{\mathcal{U}} \) and \( {\mathrm{S}}^{\mathcal{I}} \) , respectively. The following takes clustering of users as an example. Let \( {d}_{vj} \) denote the \( \left( {v,j}\right) \) -th element of matrix \( {\mathrm{S}}^{\mathcal{U}} \) . Subsequently, we assign different weights to different micro nodes. We define a merging preference score baseline \( {s}_{\text{ base }} \) for node \( v \) ,such that if the sum of the merging preference score values exceeding \( {s}_{\text{ base }} \) surpasses a preset threshold \( {\delta }_{1} \) ,the node is considered active,and a relatively high weight \( {w}_{\text{ high }} \) is assigned. Conversely,if the sum falls below a certain value \( {\delta }_{2}\left( {{\delta }_{2} \leq {\delta }_{1}}\right) \) ,the node is regarded as inactive, and a relatively low weight \( {w}_{\text{ low }} \) is assigned. For all other cases, a weight of 1 is assigned. Mathematically, the weight assigned to micro nodes \( v \) is defined as: \[{w}_{v} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} {w}_{\text{ high }}, & \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{\mathbb{1}}_{\left\{ {d}_{vj} \geq {s}_{\text{ base }}\right\} } \geq {\delta }_{1} \\ {w}_{\text{ low }}, & \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j = 1}}^{n}{\mathbb{1}}_{\left\{ {d}_{vj} \geq {s}_{\text{ base }}\right\} } \leq {\delta }_{2}, \\ 1, & \text{ otherwise } \end{array}\right. \tag{8}\] where \( {\mathbb{1}}_{\{ \cdot \} } \) denotes the indicator function. Then,the centroid update formula of preference-based grouping can be expressed as: \[{\mu }_{k} = \frac{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{v \in {\mathcal{V}}_{k}}}{w}_{v} \cdot {\mathrm{d}}_{v}}{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{v \in {\mathcal{V}}_{k}}}{w}_{v}} \tag{9}\] where \( {\mathbf{\mu }}_{k} \) is the centroid of cluster \( k,{\mathcal{V}}_{k} \) denotes the set of micro-nodes assigned to cluster \( k,{w}_{v} \) is the weight associated with node \( v \) , and \( {\mathbf{d}}_{v} = {\left( {d}_{v1},{d}_{v2}\cdots ,{d}_{vn}\right) }^{\top } \) is the \( v \) -th row of \( {\mathrm{S}}^{\mathcal{U}} \) . The clustering of items can be performed using the same method based on \( {\mathrm{S}}^{I} \) . Preference-based grouping ensures that micro-nodes with larger weights exert greater influence on the centroid's position, thereby making the centroid determination more flexible and better aligned with users' actual interests and task patterns. Macro Edge Construction. Within the MTMG, macro edges illustrate the interactions between pairs of macro nodes within defined user or item subgraphs, signifying the task trends within these subgraphs. Unlike micro edges, which link predetermined user and item nodes, macro edges are designed to adaptively represent the varying strengths of connections between two macro nodes, customized for each user or item. Specifically, we formalize the entire macro nodes set in the MTMG as \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}}_{\mathrm{{MTMG}}} = \left\{ {{\mathcal{V}}_{{k}_{1}},{\mathcal{V}}_{{k}_{2}},\ldots ,{\mathcal{V}}_{{k}_{\widetilde{m} + \widetilde{n}}}}\right\} \) with \( \widetilde{m} \) and \( \widetilde{n} \) denote the number of user clusters and item clusters, respectively. For any node \( v \) and its \( {j}^{\text{ th }} \) -hop neighbors,the weight of the macro edges is denoted by: \[{\widetilde{\mathrm{S}}}_{v;\widetilde{p},\widetilde{q}}^{\left( j\right) } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{a \in {\mathcal{V}}_{v;\widetilde{p}}^{\left( j - 1\right) }}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{b \in {\mathcal{V}}_{v;\widetilde{q}}^{\left( j\right) }}}{s}_{ab}, \tag{10}\] where \( {\mathcal{V}}_{v;\bar{p}}^{\left( j - 1\right) } = {\mathcal{V}}_{v;\bar{p}} \cap {\mathcal{N}}_{v}^{\left( j - 1\right) } \) denotes the macro nodes related to node \( v \) within its \( {\left( j - 1\right) }^{\text{ th }} \) -hop neighbors and \( {\mathcal{V}}_{v;\bar{q}}^{\left( j\right) } = {\mathcal{V}}_{v;\bar{q}} \cap {\mathcal{N}}_{v}^{\left( j\right) } \) represent the macro nodes related to node \( v \) within its \( {j}^{\text{ th }} \) -hop neighbors. By merging different task combinations, MTMG provides a macro-level view of user-item interactions. This approach allows us to observe overarching trends and structures that might not be evident from individual interactions alone. Macro Task Merging Graph Definition. Our proposed MTMG can be formally defined as \( {\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}}_{\text{ MTMG }} = \left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{U}},\widetilde{\mathcal{I}},\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}}\right) \) ,where \( \widetilde{\mathcal{U}} \) represents the set of macro user nodes and \( \widetilde{I} \) denotes set of the macro item nodes. Each macro node is associated with a trainable macro embedding \( \widetilde{\mathbf{E}} \) ,and its macro neighbors are represented as \( \widetilde{\mathcal{N}} \) . MTMG captures task patterns from a macro perspective and provides macro graph information for the subsequent macro graph bottom. ### 3.2 Macro Graph Bottom In this paper, we propose the macro graph bottom (MGB) with a mixture of macro graph experts (MGE) to exploit rich information from a macro perspective. In MGB,for each task \( t \) and a certain node \( v \) ,we assign task-specific macro embeddings to adequately capture the unique macro characteristics: \[\widetilde{{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{t}} = \operatorname{Lookup}\left( {v,{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}}_{t}}\right) \tag{11}\] where \( \widetilde{{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{t}} \) represent the macro embeddings. In addition to its own micro features, MGB applies the tailored MGEs to extract information from macro neighbors, achieving a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships and interactions between entities in MTMG from a macro perspective. For a given user-item pair from \( {\mathcal{D}}_{t} \) in MTMG,the input of MGB is concatenated by its micro embedding and macro neighbors embedding: \[{z}_{t} = \left\lbrack {{\mathbf{e}}_{u};{\mathbf{e}}_{i};{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}}_{t}\left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}_{u}\right) ;{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}}_{t}\left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}_{i}\right) }\right\rbrack , \tag{12}\] where \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{i} \) represents the original micro features and \( {\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}}_{b}\left( {\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}_{v}\right) \) denotes the corresponding macro embeddings of \( v \) ’s macro neighbors,and the task \( t \) output of MGB is illustrated as follow: \[\operatorname{MGB}\left( {{\mathcal{D}}_{t},\widetilde{\mathbb{E}},\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{{t}^{\prime } \in \mathcal{T}}}{\operatorname{Gate}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\mathbf{z}}_{t}\right) \cdot {\operatorname{MGE}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\mathbf{z}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\right) , \tag{13}\] where \( {\operatorname{Gate}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( \cdot \right) \) denotes the gating network operation,and \( {\operatorname{MGE}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( \cdot \right) \) is defined as Equation 17. \( \mathrm{{MGB}}\left( \cdot \right) \) integrates user and item embed-dings with their corresponding macro neighbor embeddings, resulting in a more informative representation that reflects the overall macro structure. ### 3.3 Macro Graph Expert Embedding-based multi-task experts, implemented using an MLP, face limitations in effectively leveraging the macro information in MTMG. We introduce a tailored MGE designed to exploit macro information efficiently. Specifically, we compute macro weights to determine the preference of the target node \( v \) with respect to its macro neighbors. These macro weights are derived from the connected macro edges. Furthermore, different task patterns can cause significant disparities in macro edge weights, which we address using logarithmic smoothing. Formally,for a target node \( v \) with its \( {j}^{\text{ th }} \) -hop macro neighbor \( \widetilde{p} \) ,we apply logarithmic smoothing with a parameter \( \gamma \) to measure the importance of these macro neighbors. The macro weight \( {w}_{v;\bar{p}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is computed as follows:

\[{w}_{v,\bar{p}}^{\left( j\right) } = \operatorname{softmax}\left( {\log \left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\bar{q} \in {\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}_{v}^{\left( j - 1\right) }}}{\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}}_{v,\bar{p},\bar{q}}^{\left( j\right) } + 1}\right) ,\gamma }\right) , \tag{14}\] where \( \gamma \) is a hyperparameter controlling the degree of smoothing [6]. To aggregate macro embeddings efficiently, we employ an attention mechanism [38] instead of computationally expensive graph convolutional neural networks. The aggregated macro embedding \( {\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}}_{v,\widetilde{p}} \) is given by: \[{\mathrm{M}}_{\mathrm{{sim}}} = \frac{\left( {{\mathrm{Q}}_{v} \cdot {\widetilde{\mathrm{E}}}_{\widetilde{p}}}\right) \cdot {\left( {\mathrm{K}}_{v} \cdot {\mathrm{E}}_{v}\right) }^{\top }}{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\widetilde{n} \in {\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}_{v}^{\left( j\right) }\smallsetminus \{ \widetilde{p}\} }}\left( {{\mathrm{Q}}_{v} \cdot {\widetilde{\mathrm{E}}}_{\widetilde{n}}}\right) \cdot {\left( {\mathrm{K}}_{v} \cdot {\mathrm{E}}_{v}\right) }^{\top }}; \tag{15}\] \[{\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}}_{v,\widetilde{p}} = \operatorname{softmax}\left( \frac{{\mathbf{M}}_{\operatorname{sim}}}{\sqrt{d}}\right) \cdot \left( {{\mathbf{V}}_{v} \cdot {\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}}_{\widetilde{p}}}\right) , \tag{16}\] where \( {\mathrm{Q}}_{v},{\mathrm{\;K}}_{v} \) and \( {\mathrm{V}}_{v} \) are learnable query,key,and value matrices for node \( v \) ,and \( {\mathbf{M}}_{\text{ sim }} \) reflects the similarity between target node \( v \) and macro nodes \( \widetilde{p} \) . Finally,the fusion of macro neighbor representations of task \( t \) is expressed as: \[{\operatorname{MGE}}_{t}\left( {z}_{t}\right) = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\widetilde{p} \in {\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}}_{o}^{\left( j\right) }}}{w}_{v,\widetilde{p}} \cdot {\widetilde{Z}}_{v,\widetilde{p}} \tag{17}\] where \( {\operatorname{MGE}}_{t}\left( {z}_{t}\right) \) represents the final output of macro graph expert. ### 3.4 Macro Prediction Tower Macro and Micro Fusion. To capture the detailed local interactions provided by micro neighbors and the broader context offered by macro neighbors, we introduce the macro and micro fusion to aggregate information from both perspectives. Specifically, for a given target node \( v \) with its numerous neighbors \( {\mathcal{N}}_{v} \) related to task \( t \) ,we sum its micro neighbors. Then, the micro neighbors representation \( {\mathbf{e}}_{v;\text{ nbr }}^{t} \) can be expressed as: \[{\mathbf{e}}_{v;\text{ nbr }}^{t} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{c \in {\mathcal{N}}_{a}}}\left\langle {{\mathbf{e}}_{c}^{t},{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{t}}\right\rangle \cdot {\mathbf{e}}_{c}^{t} \tag{18}\] where \( \left\langle {{\mathbf{e}}_{c}^{t},{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{t}}\right\rangle \) indicates the weight between the target node and its micro neighbors. Then, we mix the macro and micro informative representations through a multi-gate expert layer: \[{\mathbf{e}}_{\text{ cat }}^{t} = \left\lbrack {{\mathbf{e}}_{u};{\mathbf{e}}_{i};\operatorname{MGB}\left( {\mathbf{z}}_{t}\right) ;{\mathbf{e}}_{u;\text{ nbr }}^{t};{\mathbf{e}}_{i;\text{ nbr }}^{t}}\right\rbrack ; \tag{19}\] \[{x}^{t} = {h}_{t}\left( {e}_{\mathrm{{cat}}}^{t}\right) \tag{20}\] where \( {\mathbf{e}}_{\text{ cat }} \) represents the concatenated embedding, \( {h}_{t}\left( \cdot \right) \) is defined as Equation 2,and \( {x}^{t} \) denotes the informative fused output from both the macro and micro levels. To exploit possible connections between tasks and fully utilize a user's macro preferences for sparse tasks, we replace the traditional multi-task tower with a macro correlated layer. Specifically, we use a macro cascading readout layer to explore the relationships across different tasks and apply macro task adjustment to align the recommendations with the user's macro preferences. Macro Cascading Readout Module. Traditional multi-task recommendation models [26, 36] obtain results in a parallel manner, which ignores the possible connections between different tasks. To address this, we introduce the macro cascading readout module that generates the final output in a cascaded fashion. Specifically, the output of the previous task is fed into the next prediction tower as additional input. Suppose \( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( {t}_{j}\right) } \) is the output of the previous task, then \( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( {t}_{j}\right) } \) can be expressed as: \[{\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( {t}_{j}\right) } = \left\{ {\begin{array}{ll} \sigma \left( {\operatorname{MLP}\left( {x}^{{t}_{1}}\right) }\right) , & {t}_{j} = {t}_{1} \\ \sigma \left( {\operatorname{MLP}\left( {x}^{{t}_{j}}\right) + {w}_{{t}_{j - 1}} \cdot {\widehat{y}}_{{t}_{j - 1}}}\right) , & {t}_{j} \in \mathcal{T} \smallsetminus \left\{ {t}_{1}\right\} \end{array},}\right. \tag{21}\] where \( {w}_{{t}_{j - 1}} \) is a trainable parameter that controls the strength of learning the correlation between different tasks. Macro Task Adjustment. With the goal of recommending more precisely to the user's individual preferences and enhancing the model's ability to predict sparse tasks, we propose macro task adjustment to guide the final prediction. First, based on MTMG, we construct a user macro task lookup table according to different task interactions. Specifically, we associate various user's task interactions with the corresponding macro nodes. For a certain user \( u \) ,the final prediction \( \widehat{\mathrm{Y}} \) can be expressed as: \[\widehat{\mathrm{Y}} = {\mathbf{W}}_{u} \cdot {\mathbf{Y}}_{\text{ cat }} = \sigma \left( {T}_{u}\right) \cdot \left\lbrack {{\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( {t}_{1}\right) };{\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{\left( {t}_{2}\right) };\ldots }\right\rbrack , \tag{22}\] where \( {T}_{u} \) is the users’ macro task lookup table, \( {\mathbf{W}}_{u} \) represents the macro task adjustment weight corresponding to the user in relation to the target item's macro node. ### 3.5 Model Training We utilize binary cross-entropy as the loss function during the model’s training. Specifically,with the loss function \( {\mathcal{L}}_{t} \) for a certain task \( t \) ,the objective of MTL is given by: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{{MTL}}} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t \in \mathcal{T}}}{\alpha }_{t}{\mathcal{L}}_{t} \tag{23}\] Then, the overall objective function for MGOE is formulated as: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{{MGOE}}} = {\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{{MTL}}} + {\lambda }_{1} \cdot \parallel \theta {\parallel }_{1} + {\lambda }_{2} \cdot \parallel \theta {\parallel }_{2}^{2}, \tag{24}\] where \( {\lambda }_{1} \cdot \parallel \theta {\parallel }_{1} \) and \( {\lambda }_{2} \cdot \parallel \theta {\parallel }_{2}^{2} \) represent the \( {\ell }_{1} \) and \( {\ell }_{2} \) regularization terms, respectively, included to prevent overfitting. ## 4 EXPERIMENTS In this section, we conduct comprehensive experiments on three real-world datasets, aiming to answer the following research questions. ### 4.1 Experimental Setup 4.1.1 Datasets. We conduct extensive experiments on three real-world benchmark datasets: Taobao [58], QB-video [46] and QK-article [46]. The detailed description and the statistics of these datasets is illustrated in B.1. 4.1.2 Compared Baselines. To verify the effectiveness of MGOE, we compare with ten relevant representative multi-task models, which can be roughly divided into two categories. (i)Traditional Multi-task Models: MMOE, PLE, ESMM, AITM, STEM, MoME. (ii) Graph-based Methods: MoGENet, MMoCEG, POGCN, MacGNN. We leave the details of these baseline models in B.2. 4.1.3 Implementation Details. All baselines and MGOE is implemented based on Pytorch. In the offline experiments, the embedding size fix to 10 and use Xavier [10] for initialization for all models. For MGOE, we set the batch size to 1024 and use Adam [23] for optimization. The learning rate is searched form \( \{ 1\mathrm{e} - 2,5\mathrm{e} - 2,1\mathrm{e} - 3 \) , 5e-3\} and the regularization term is searched form \( \{ 1\mathrm{e} - 4,5\mathrm{e} - 5,1\mathrm{e} - 5\} \) . 4.1.4 Evaluation Metrics. We adopt two widely used multi-task evaluation metrics, AUC [8] and Logloss [5], for a comprehensive evaluation of the models. Higher values of AUC indicate better prediction performance of the model, while the lower values of Logloss imply better prediction accuracy. Higher values of AUC indicate better CTR prediction performance of the model, while the lower values of Logloss indicate better CTR prediction performance. We run the experiments five times with different random seeds and take the average result to avoid extreme cases. ### 4.2 Main Results (RQ1) In this subsection, we compare our tailored MGOE with ten state-of-the-art baseline models on three experimental datasets. In this experiment, our model served as a rank model, replacing the existing online best-performed ranking models-MMOE and MacGNN. MacGNN mainly considers the clicking task, MMOE and MGOE consider "clicking", "adding to cart", "favoring", and "buying". Compared to MMOE, firstly, MGOE demonstrates a performance improvement of 2.16% for PCTR, 1.63% for UCTR, 5.88% for CVR, and 16.46% for GMV, suggesting that our model boosts users' inclination to interact with items and turn them into purchases. Secondly, the StayTime increases by \( {4.12}\% \) . This indicates that,despite both models considering a wide range of user actions, by incorporating their comprehensive macro interests, our model is more effective in attracting user clicks and driving business revenue. Compared to MacGNN, which has a more narrow focus on clicking task, our model still shows favorable performance. The PCTR increased by \( {0.93}\% \) ,the UCTR rose by \( {0.75}\% \) ,the CVR increased by 3.69%, the GMV grew by 7.74%, and the user StayTime increased by 3.26%. This suggests that the broader consideration of user actions in MGOE can lead to better overall business outcomes, even when compared to a model specialized in a single task. Overall, in the online A/B test on the Alibaba platform, all the results show that MTMG and the equipped MGOE are more suitable than the state-of-the-art online multi-task recommendation models. ## 5 CONCLUSION The introduction of the Macro Task Merging Graph (MTMG) and Macro Graph of Experts (MGOE) not only significantly advances the field of multi-task graph-based recommendation but also has practical implications for improving the performance of large-scale recommender systems. MTMG merges multiple billion-scale graphs into a unified macro structure, effectively consolidating complex graph data. MGOE leverages macro graph embeddings with macro graph experts, which provides a novel approach for integrating macro graph information and enables more efficient information extraction. Extensive offline experiments and online A/B tests demonstrate the superiority of our model.

## A RELATED WORK ### A.1 Multi-task Learning Multi-task learning aims to enhance the model's generalization ability by training multiple tasks concurrently within the same model. The core of this method lies in the knowledge that can be shared among different tasks, enabling them to benefit from one another. In the early days of deep learning, the hard sharing mechanism of parameters was commonly employed. It could be applied to all hidden layers for all tasks, while maintaining task-specific output layers. The parameter soft sharing mechanism, on the other hand, allows each task to have its own model and parameters, thereby achieving better performance. The cross-stitch network utilizes the cross-stitch unit to take a task-specific network and linearly combine it with the previous output by leveraging knowledge learned from other tasks. However, in recommendation systems, parameter sharing between tasks that have poor correlation can lead to a seesaw phenomenon. To solve the issues of data sparsity (DS) and sample selection bias (SSB), ESSM [27] simultaneously optimizes two related tasks in a sequential manner. MOE [21] employs a gated network to transform the original parameters shared by all samples into multiple sets of parameters, where each set is called an expert. MMOE [26] proposes a multi-expert network to address the multi-task learning problem, with the hope that the model could automatically learn to assign expert parameters based on the relationship of the underlying task. PLE [36] divides the model parameters into a private part and a shared part, which improves the robustness of multi-task learning and mitigates the negative impact between private knowledge and shared knowledge. ### A.2 Graph Learning for Recommendation In recent years, an increasing number of studies have attempted to integrate graphs into recommendation systems in order to enhance performance. NGCF [42] typically incorporates higher-order graph information into traditional collaborative filtering. To achieve superior performance, LightGCN [13] removes non-linear operations and feature transformations, which are found to be redundant through experimentation. These methods have been widely adopted in industrial item recall scenarios. However, due to their long inference times, these methods are difficult to apply directly to multi-task learning. Subsequently, some approaches attempt to incorporate graph information into the CTR prediction scenario. MoGENet [18] proposes a novel multi-channel graph neural network to jointly model high-order information using the user-item bipartite graph. MMoCEG [48] utilizes a graph-based structure to share information across regions and employs contrastive learning to prevent expert representation degeneration. GLSM [35] employs an adaptive fusion mechanism to fuse information from long-term and short-term behaviors. GMT [28] effectively integrates different types of interactions between local neighborhood nodes from both explicit and implicit perspectives to generate highly representative embeddings for the target user-item pair. MacGNN [4] attempts to cluster similar micro nodes into a macro node to reduce computational complexity. ### A.3 Click-Through Rate Prediction Click-Through Rate (CTR) Prediction is one of the core algorithms in the recommendation system \( \left\lbrack {{52},{60}}\right\rbrack \) ,which predicts whether a user will click on an advertisement or not. The CTR prediction is influenced by the user's historical click-through rate and behavior, and it is trained on vast amounts of historical data by combining various factors and characteristics. Traditional shallow CTR models, such as Logistic Regression (LR), Degree-2 Polynomial Mappings (Poly2), and Factorization Machine (FM) [30], were widely used in the early days due to their lightweight nature and strong interpretability. With the development of deep learning, modern deep learning methods have achieved significant improvements. FNN uses FM in the embedding layer to generate hidden vectors as initialization values for embeddings. PNN [29] adds a product layer between the embedding layer and the MLP. By adding an attention mechanism between the embedding layer and the MLP, DIN [57] can learn from the user's past behavior. DIEN [56] incorporates the ARGRU sequence model to model the evolution process of interest. DeepFM [11] replaces LR in the traditional wide part with FM, and DCN [39] further replaces FM with a cross layer network to handle feature crossover. DCNv2 [40] uses low-rank mixing to strike a balance between performance and delay, thereby achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. ## B EXPERIMENTAL DETAILS ### B.1 Dataset Details We adopt three publicly available datasets for offline evaluation. ### B.2 Baseline Details We compare our proposed MGOE with ten relevant representative multi-task models, which can be roughly divided into two categories. ## (I) Traditional Multi-task Models: - MMoE [26] introduces a gating network to assign different expert networks to different tasks, allowing the model to share knowledge between different tasks while retaining the task-specific information processing ability. - PLE [36] extracts deep information layer by separating shared experts and task specific experts, which helps to solve the negative transfer problem and seesaw problem in multi-task learning. - ESMM [27] effectively solves the problem of data sparsity and sample selection bias in CVR estimation, and improves the generalization ability of the model by training on the entire sample space. - AITM [44] proposes an adaptive information transfer multitask framework to models the sequence dependencies between user multi-step transitions through an adaptive information transfer module. - STEM [34] proposes a novel share and task-specific embedding paradigm and it is equipped with an all forward task-specific backward gating network to facilitate the learning of task-specific embeddings and direct knowledge transfer across tasks. - MoME [45] designs an expert to share parameter efficiently and achieve resource utilization. It extracts from an identical over-parameterized base network by utilizing a binary mask learning mechanism composed of neuron-level model masking and weight-level expert masking. ## (II) Graph-based Methods: - MoGENet [18] introduce a multi-channel graph neural network module designed to adaptively extract the most pertinent and significant information from the bipartite graph. - MMoCEG [48] addresses the expert representation degeneration problem through contrastive learning, and introduces a graph-based gating mechanism to recognize the commonalities and differences among multiple regions. - POGCN [53] introduces partial order graphs to unify separate behavior graphs into a joint graph, leveraging graph convolutional networks to aggregate neighbor information while considering behavior relations. - MacGNN [4] resolves the computational complexity problems in the infrastructure by reducing the node count from billions to hundreds, it improves the accuracy of CTR prediction while remaining computationally efficient.
